core: Definition of an incentive as anything that changes the costs or benefits of an action
The principle that people respond to incentives in predictable ways
How prices, taxes, subsidies, and penalties function as incentives
Unintended consequences and perverse incentives, with a carefully framed real example
One concrete policy that changed behavior through incentives (cigarette excise tax)
supporting: Prices as signals that coordinate buyers and sellers
The cost-benefit basis for why incentives work (rational agents comparing costs and benefits)

claims.claim: An incentive is anything that changes the costs or benefits of an action and thereby motivates behavior; a core economic principle is that people respond to incentives in predictable ways.
Incentives can be positive (rewards that make an action more attractive) or negative (penalties that make it less attractive), and changes in incentives cause people to change behavior predictably.
Prices, and the taxes and subsidies that alter them, act as incentives: laws that control prices change the incentives facing buyers and firms and often produce undesirable consequences.

The U.S. Congressional Budget Office estimated that a 10 percent increase in cigarette prices leads people under 18 to reduce smoking by about 5 to 15 percent and adults over 18 to reduce it by about 3 to 7 percent, illustrating a tax changing behavior through incentives.

Poorly designed incentives can be perverse: a bounty paid per unit of a proxy (e.g., severed rat tails in 1902 French colonial Hanoi) rewarded catching-and-releasing or breeding the pest rather than eliminating it.

The term 'cobra effect' was coined by economist Horst Siebert (2001) from a British-Raj anecdote about a cobra bounty; the anecdote is historically unverified/disputed, whereas the 1902 Hanoi rat-tail bounty is documented by historian Michael G. Vann (2003).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Historical accuracy of the classic 'cobra effect' anecdote used to teach perverse incentives.
positions: The Delhi cobra-bounty story is a widely repeated illustration coined by Siebert (2001).
A 2025 Friends of Snakes Society investigation and an 1887 Bombay Natural History Society inquiry found no documentation of cobra-breeding-for-bounty, calling the anecdote historically unsupported.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the 'cobra effect' as the popular label but presents it as illustrative/disputed, and uses the well-documented 1902 Hanoi rat-tail bounty (Vann 2003) as the concrete historical example.
